China's Xi Jinping places himself firmly in the center of the trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. Doug Mills/Getty Images It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. item.title: What are the implications of the ICJ Rohingya genocide ruling?
item.description:
A Rohingya refugee waves Myanmar's national flag as he waits for the arrival of U.N. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 20, 2026. —Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty Images The world’s top international court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority, more than a million of whom remain displaced. The verdict , issued Thursday, is the first time a state has been found responsible for committing genocide in the history of the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945. In a weekslong military campaign in 2017, Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 people, including up to 2,109 children under five, and forced more than 700,000 others to flee the country’s northern Rakhine State. item.title: Myanmar is the first state found responsible for genocide. Here's how the ICJ ruled in other cases
item.description:
International Court of Justice President Iwasawa Yuji reads the court's judgment in The Hague on Nov. 19, 2026. Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images The International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not. The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar. But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have important effects on the court’s other ongoing genocide cases,…

item.title: COP31 wrapping up in Turkey: Climate deal elusive as fossil fuels go unmentioned
item.description:
The UN's COP31 climate talks were set to spill into overtime Friday as countries remained deadlocked over a draft deal that makes no mention of fossil fuels, with a host of other disputes also snarling negotiations. The talks come with a series of stark reminders of the urgency of climate action, from heatwaves in Europe and devastating floods in Nepal, while a record-breaking El Nino supercharges temperatures. FRANCE 24's Environment Editor Valerie Dekimpe tells us more.

item.title: Welcome to Software Beirut
item.description:
Last week, when it briefly looked like the world was collapsing while I sat on the tarmac, I wrote about the arrival of Software Beirut —“where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time, and the main skill you need is not being surprised.” I’m no Tom Friedman , but many people seemed to enjoy the phrase and encouraged me to keep using it even as outages at the FAA, Chase, and Microsoft proved to be isolated incidents unrelated to bad guys using advanced AI. Well, hold my mustache wax! Because I’m doubling down. The fact that all of the software chaos appears to have had boring causes doesn’t negate my point—it improves it. Software Beirut is not an event but an environment, shaped by three forces that arrived at roughly the same time: AI is exposing vulnerabilities in critical software at unprecedented speed; the rush to fix the bugs creates its own hair ball…

item.title: Court grants request to prevent military from detonating bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
item.description:
Update, November 19: Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle has announced that the detonation will be postponed until November 23. On Friday, the US Army is scheduled to detonate roughly 11,000 pounds of lead azide, an unstable bomb-making chemical, in southeastern Iowa. The explosion will send a plume of lead-contaminated dust across a hundred-mile swath of the Midwest. Though the Army reportedly knew of the potential hazard for years, residents of the 400-person community of Middletown, who will be expected to evacuate, were given just a month’s notice of the plan to ignite 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.
